name: Posture awareness

lead: Posture awareness means noticing and correcting slouching, rounded shoulders and a forward head, so you look taller, more open and more confident.

Keeping the head over the shoulders and the spine upright counters the head-forward posture of phone and desk use. Research on posture mostly covers back and neck pain and ergonomics, including a school trial of a back education programme and a 2024 study of a photographic method for making posture actionable.

paras: People use mirrors, side-on photos, reminders and feedback to check their stance, often alongside strengthening work for the back and core. The change in stance is visible while held, and habits build over weeks.
Low risk. Persistent pain or a visible spinal curve is a matter for a clinician.

angle.text: Keeping your head over your shoulders and your spine upright counters the forward-head posture of phone and desk use, so you look taller and more present. The change is visible while held, and posture research has focused on pain rather than attractiveness.

lead: Posture awareness is the practice of noticing and correcting how one stands and sits, for example keeping the head over the shoulders and the spine upright. In appearance-focused communities it is discussed as a way to look taller, more confident and more "present", and to counter the head-forward posture associated with phone and desk use.

Published research on posture awareness mostly concerns health outcomes. A cluster-randomised school trial of a back education programme that included posture awareness training examined back pain and back behaviour in children,[1] and a 2024 study described a photographic method for making posture actionable.[2] No published trial found in this review tests posture awareness for changing perceived attractiveness or presence.
infobox: Noticing and adjusting standing and sitting posture
Forward head posture, power posing, body language

paras: Quiet standing involves continuous small sway at the ankles, often modelled as an inverted pendulum.[3] Perceptual studies suggest touch information from the soles of the feet contributes to the brain's sense of body posture.[4] Posture awareness, in the self-improvement sense, adds deliberate attention to alignment.

Wikipedia describes forward head posture as the head sitting forward of the shoulders, commonly linked to long periods of hunching over laptops and phones, and notes that rounded shoulders with forward head are called upper crossed syndrome.[5] A 2019 meta-analysis cited there found a relationship between forward head posture and neck pain in adults but not in adolescents.[5] The same article carries tags noting that it needs better medical references.[5]

Body-language references report that a fuller, forward chest is associated with confidence and a pulled-back chest with less confidence, and that leaning forward suggests openness.[6] Posture is also context-dependent: the same stance may read differently across cultures.[6]

A cluster-randomised controlled study of 176 children aged 10 to 12 tested a teacher-led back education programme with knowledge improvement, posture awareness training and reduction of muscular imbalance over 10 months, assessing back pain, motor skills, back behaviour and knowledge.[1] A randomised trial of 62 adults with non-specific chronic neck pain compared manual therapy plus exercise with exercise alone over three weeks, with both groups given strengthening exercises for neck and scapular stability.[7] A 2022 literature review examined physiotherapeutic scoliosis-specific exercise methods and their effectiveness.[8] Titles of further studies cover posture feedback training and health,[9] and tech neck symptoms in a pilot questionnaire.[10] These studies concern pain, health or ergonomics rather than attractiveness.
